newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Japan fiscal policy debate focus wrong-Nomura.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Japan fiscal policy debate focus wrong-Nomura.

text.p: The current fiscal policy debate in Japan was focused in the wrong direction, a senior economist of a leading Japanese security house said today.

If the government were to cut back public spending as a means of reining in the deficit, it would risk pulling out the only pillar currently supporting the Japanese economy, Richard Koo, chief economist of the Nomura Research Institute in Tokyo, told a seminar in Sydney.
With corporate demand for funds having collapsed in Japan, the fact that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) had cut interest rates to historically low levels waS irrelevant, as no one was borrowing.
"So the real debate in Japan should be a review of what to spend the money on, not whether to spend the money or not, because it has to be spent to keep the Japanese economy going," Koo said.
When the BOJ cut the discount rate to 0.5 percent in December 1995, it increased the liquidity in the economy as a means of helping the economy around a banking crisis, he said.
As this was expected to boost growth, equities were bought, and Japanese bonds (JGBs) were shorted by foreign investors in anticipations of higher growth driving yields up.

And while the Nikkei rose, the JGB market did not collapse. Instead it rallied, and investors found the reason the Japanese were buying 10-year bonds at 2.3 percent was because corporate demand for funds had collapsed, and so no one would take their money.
"The fact that there are no borrowers for funds in Japan means Bank of Japan monetary policy has not been working," Koo said.
The problem was that despite the historically low interest rates, borrowers were still noticeably absent, rendering monetary policy ineffective and leaving Japan in a liquidity trap.
All that had been keeping the Japanese economy going then had been fiscal policy, which was now under threat as the government sought to reign in the budget deficit.

The problem for the goverment was that high public spending was becoming unpopular with taxpayers, who were seeing little benefit from the large amounts of public spending and were tiring of funding it.

"What you've had there over the last few years is the building of a whole bunch of usless projects, and that's where the taxpayer revolts have come in -- but coming in at exactly at the worst possible moment," Koo said.
This had left markets concerned that if the fiscal stimulus was withdrawn, the Japanese economy would collapse, and this was reflected in the ongoing low yields for JGBs.

"And that's where some if the concerns in the market come from...if that's the only pillar keeping the Japanese economy going, you cut this one off and the whole house will come crashing down," he said.

So the debate should be about how to use the public spending, rather than whether to cut it back, when the government had been presented with an opportunity to provide infrastructure, in a time of low interest rates and with little chance of the crowding out of the private sector occuring.
"But unfortunately the debate is totally elsewhere and I think that is what is bothering the markets, particularly the bond market," Koo said.
